title: Atmosphere and Climate
intro:
What do you see when you look up in the sky? You might see the
floating clouds, the sunshine, and feel a breeze as well. All of these
are a result of a blanket of air surrounding the Earth, called the
atmosphere. It is pulled down around the Earth by gravity, and
is a mixture of gases in various proportions, vital for the survival
of all living beings on the Earth. The atmosphere shields us from
the harmful radiation coming from the Sun, including ultraviolet
radiation. It regulates the Earth's temperature by trapping some of
the Sun's energy and prevents it from escaping back into space. The
atmosphere is a key component of the Earth's weather and climate
systems, influencing factors such as temperature, humidity, and
air pressure.

sections.title: Composition of the Atmosphere
sections.content:
The Earth's atmosphere is composed of a mixture of various gases.
Nitrogen and oxygen are the two primary and most abundant
gases that are essential to life on the Earth. Carbon dioxide, argon,
helium, neon, krypton, xenon, ozone, and hydrogen are some other
gases present in the atmosphere, but are found in lesser quantities.
Besides these, the atmosphere also consists of water vapour and
tiny dust particles. The amount of water vapour in the atmosphere
varies, but it generally ranges from 0.1 per cent to 0.4 per cent. It
plays a significant role in cloud formation and precipitation. The
composition of the atmosphere also varies with altitude.

sections.content:
'Is it going to rain today?' 'Will it be bright and sunny today?' How
often do you find yourself wondering about these questions when
you want to go out and play?
The term weather refers to the hour-to-hour and day-to-day
conditions of the atmosphere. Hot or humid weather may make one
irritable, while pleasant or breezy weather may make one cheerful,
or even plan for an outing. Weather can vary significantly from
day-to-day. The average weather conditions of a place over a longer
period of time refer to the climate of the place. Climate refers to the
sum total of weather conditions and variations over a large area for
an extended period of time, usually thirty years or more.

sections.title: Seasons in India
sections.content:
The climate of India can be broadly classified as tropical monsoon.
The Indian Meteorological Department (IMD) has recognised four
distinct seasons in India:

 Winter: The winter season generally lasts from December to

early April. The coldest months of the year are December and
January, when the average temperature in the north-west is
around 10-15°C. Temperatures increase towards the equator,
reaching around 20-25°C in mainland India's south-east.

 Summer or pre-monsoon: The summer or pre-monsoon season
spans from April to June, or up to July in north-western India.
In western and southern regions, the hottest month is April; in
northern regions, it is May. The average temperature across most
of inland India ranges from 32-40°C.

 Monsoon or rainy (Advancing monsoon):

The monsoon
season generally spans from June to September. This season is
dominated by the humid south-west summer monsoon, which
slowly sweeps across the country in late May or early June.
Monsoon rain begins to recede from north India at the beginning
of October, and South India typically receives more rainfall
during this time.

 Post-monsoon (Retreating monsoon): The post-monsoon
season lasts from October to December. In north-western India,
October and November are usually cloudless.

The Himalayan states, being more temperate, experience two
additional seasons, autumn and spring.

sections.content:
In an economy, the answers to these three key questions depend on
how the resources used to produce goods and services are organised
and who controls the decision-making regarding them. The system
that defines the mechanisms for the production, consumption, and
distribution of goods, services, and resources is known as the
economic system of a country.
Understanding Society:
India and Beyond
Grade 9 - Part 1

The three kinds of economic systems are explained in the following
pages.

190

Chapter 8.indd 190

 Planned Economy
In a planned economy, a central planning authority of the
government, such as the planning commission, makes all major
economic decisions in the market, that is, what and how much will be
produced, how they will be produced, and who will get to use them
and at what prices. The government has ownership in most resources
and sectors like land, factories, banks, and transport. With limited
private ownership, enterprises usually follow the central authority's
targets rather than market demand, and are heavily regulated by the
government through strict permits and licenses to produce goods
and services. However, this prevents a large number of enterprises to
operate in the market and thus restricts competition among private
enterprises. As a result, there is little motivation among enterprises to
improve quality or innovate. Some examples of planned economies
are the former Soviet Union, North Korea, and Cuba.

Market Economy
In a market economy, the questions of what, how, and how much to
produce are addressed mainly by the forces of demand and supply
with little government intervention. Often, the government acts like
a referee in a football match. It ensures safety and law and order, and
it does not control prices or production. The ownership of factories,
shops, land, and other resources, largely rests with individuals and
private companies. Many producers offer similar products, which
encourages better quality, lower prices, and innovation in production
of goods and services. Some of the prominent examples include
the United States of America, Japan, and Hong Kong. However,
governments play an important role even in these economies.

sections.title: Other Determinants of Demand
sections.content:
When a new model of a popular smartphone is launched, long
queues and pre-bookings indicate the rush to buy it, even if it is more
expensive. So, the demand for a product does not necessarily change
only because of price. Many other factors influence how much people
want to buy, even when the price of the good or service remains the
same. Let us see some of these factors at play.
Related goods:
Products whose
demand is
interconnected,
meaning a change
in the price or
availability of one
directly affects
the demand for
the other.

Understanding Society:
India and Beyond

Price of related goods
The demand for a good can be affected by changes in the prices of
related goods. There are two types of related goods:
a)

Substitute goods - These goods can replace each other, like tea
and coffee. If tea's price remains the same while coffee becomes
more expensive, people who consume coffee may switch to
tea, thereby increasing its demand. If Srivalli cannot afford
to buy mangoes at the market price, she may buy bananas.
When the price of a good rises, people tend to replace it with
another relatively cheaper alternative. Hence, if the price of
the substitute good increases, the demand for the other related
good will increase.

b)

Complementary goods - These goods are generally used together
to provide utility to the consumer, for instance, smartphones
and earphones, or cars and petrol. If the demand for printers
increases, the demand for printer cartridges may also rise, even
though the price of cartridges remains unchanged. Similarly, if
movie tickets become more expensive, people may refrain from
going to the cinema, so demand for popcorn sold in cinema halls
may also fall.

 Income of the consumer
When household income rises, consumers can afford to buy more
or choose higher-quality products. A rise in income generally makes
people feel more confident about their ability to spend, so the
quantity demanded for several goods rises, even if prices remain
the same.

Taste and preference of the buyer
Every consumer has specific tastes and preferences for certain
products, which determine their demand. For example, Srivalli likes
mangoes and cannot substitute them by oranges, even if oranges are
cheaper than mangoes.
The demand also depends on the size and composition of the nation's
population. For example, being the most populous nation, India's
domestic consumer demand contributes to its economic growth.
In addition, the population's composition shapes the demand for
types of products and services.

to offer at a particular price. As price increases, quantity supplied
increases, and as price decreases, quantity supplied falls. This is
because higher prices increase profitability, incentivising producers
to increase output, and also attract new firms to the market. This
is known as the law of supply. Individual supply is the quantity a
particular seller offers at different prices.

Public goods are goods and services that are provided by the
government for the benefit of all citizens, for example, roads,
bridges, public parks, and streetlighting are provided for public
use; national defence protects the country from external threats;

Suppose your neighbourhood needs a park. Building it is expensive,

paying.” Because of this thinking, not enough money is collected, and

why goods that benefit everyone often require government provision

sections.title: Ocean Currents
sections.content:
Ocean currents are continuous streams of water that flow across
the ocean surface in definite directions (). They are caused
by factors, such as winds, the Earth's rotation (Coriolis force),
differences in temperature and salinity, and the shape of continents
and ocean basins. Ocean currents may be warm or cold depending
on the direction from which the water flows. Currents flowing from
warmer regions are called warm currents, while those flowing from
colder regions are called cold currents. On maps, warm currents are
usually shown in red and cold currents in blue.

THINK ABOUT IT
Observe the map carefully and note the movement patterns of
cold and warm currents. Do you think these currents affect the
temperature of nearby coastal regions?
The Gulf Stream, a warm current originating in the Gulf of Mexico
in the Atlantic Ocean, flows towards Norway and keeps its waters
relatively warm. As a result, sea ice does not form easily in the
Norwegian region despite its high latitude (60°-70°). In contrast,
the Labrador Current, a cold current flowing along the east coast of
Canada, carries freezing water and supports the formation of sea ice
and icebergs even at lower latitudes.

Oceans and seas can give rise to sudden natural hazards such as

dangers, scientists have developed Early Warning Systems that work
like giant alarm systems for coastal areas. To reduce risks, people,

issue timely warnings so that people can evacuate and stay safe.

The sea area closest to a country is called its territorial waters, over
which the country has near-complete control, subject to the right of
innocent passage for foreign ships. Just as on land, the government
can make laws relating to customs, immigration, and pollution
control in this zone.

Innocent Passage is a principle that allows foreign ships to pass
through the territorial waters of a country as long as they do
not threaten its peace, good order, or security. Ships must move
continuously without stopping, except in emergencies or cases of
breakdowns. This right does not permit activities such as fishing,
military operations, or other non-peaceful actions.
Beyond the contiguous zone, lie the Exclusive Economic Zones
(EEZs), which extend from the baseline up to 200 nautical miles from
the coast, and are defined under the United Nations Convention on
the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS) by global agreement. In these zones, a
country has special rights to use ocean resources, such as fish, oil,
and gas, although ships from other countries may still pass through
peacefully. It is important to note, however, that the country does not
fully own or control the waters of the EEZ.
Beyond the EEZs of all countries lie the high seas, also known as
international waters. Covering about 64 per cent of the world's
oceans, these waters do not belong to any single country and are
therefore considered part of the global commons. All countries enjoy
equal rights on the high seas, including navigation, fishing, flying
over them, laying undersea cables, building lawful structures such
as artificial lands, and exploring for minerals.

sections.title: International Maritime Rules and Regulations
sections.content:
In the earlier sections of this chapter, you learnt that oceans are
vital for trade, travel, and communication. To ensure that activities
at sea remain safe, fair, and peaceful, countries follow a set of
international rules and agreements known as maritime law or
maritime regulations. These laws regulate how ships operate and
move; protect the marine environment; address issues such as
piracy, terrorism, natural disasters, and accidents; safeguard trade
routes; and help settle disputes between countries.

LET'S EXPLORE
Maritime disputes are conflicts or disagreements between
countries over territory, resources, or rights in naval areas such as
oceans, seas, or coastal regions. Can you find out some countries
that have conflicts over their territorial sea waters?

Important Maritime Rules and Regulations
Just as there are traffic rules on land, ships must follow “rules of
the road at sea” to avoid accidents. These rules, known as COLREGs
(Convention on the International Regulations for Preventing
Collisions at Sea), include maintaining a proper lookout, deciding
which side to pass on, identifying the give-way and stand-on vessels,
proceeding at a safe speed, and using lights, sound signals, shapes
(for different types of vessels such as fishing boats), along with
appropriate actions to prevent collisions. In addition, ships use
international signals and radio communication to share information
and prevent accidents, especially in crowded or hazardous waters.

 Ships must also meet safety standards and are prohibited from
polluting the seas. The MARPOL (International Convention for the
Prevention of Pollution from Ships) Convention is an important
international agreement aimed at reducing pollution from ships.

Why are Maritime Rules Important?
International maritime rules, regulations, and agreements help keep
the oceans safe and ensure the fair and sustainable use of ocean
resources. These rules enable countries to cooperate in using marine
resources without conflict while protecting marine life, ships, sailors,
and coastal communities. Without such regulations, the oceans could
become dangerous and chaotic, with increased pollution, accidents,
collisions, and disputes over resources. By establishing common
standards for all ships, regardless of the country they belong to,
maritime rules help keep the oceans safe, clean, and open for trade
and travel.

sections.title: Interconnectedness between Biomes and Living Beings
sections.content:
Interconnectedness between Biomes
and Living Beings
Biomes are closely connected to living beings because they provide
a natural environment where plants, animals, and humans can
survive and interact. At the same time, living beings also influence
biomes-animals help in pollination and seed dispersal, humans
modify landscapes for farming or cities, and microorganisms recycle
nutrients. In this way, biomes and living beings are interconnected
systems that depend on one another to maintain ecological balance
and biodiversity. We will discuss some of the aspects of this
interconnectedness in the following section.

Maintaining Ecological Balance and Biodiversity

sections.title: Biodiversity
sections.content:
Biodiversity is the variety of life on Earth,
including plants, animals, microorganisms,
and the ecosystems they inhabit ().
It refers not only to the number of different
species but also to the genetic differences
within species and the variety of habitats
and ecological processes that sustain life.
In simple terms, biodiversity means the
richness of life forms and the natural
balance they create, which is essential
for maintaining healthy ecosystems and
supporting human survival.

 The geographical aspects of biodiversity conservation focus on
how location, climate, landforms, and ecosystems influence the
protection and management of living organisms. Since biodiversity
is unevenly distributed across the Earth, geography plays a vital role
in conservation. Some key aspects of conservation are-
Hotspots of Biodiversity: Certain regions, such as the Himalaya,
the Western Ghats, the North-East India, and the Andaman & Nicobar
Islands, are rich in unique species found nowhere else. Identifying
and protecting these hotspots is a priority in conservation.

Ecosystem-Based Conservation: Different biomes (forests, wetlands,
deserts, coasts, and mountains) support distinct life forms. Conservation
strategies must suit the geographical setting; for example, mangrove
protection along coasts or afforestation in mountains.
Protected Areas: National parks, wildlife sanctuaries, biosphere
reserves, and World Heritage Sites are chosen based on geography
to preserve critical habitats and prevent habitat fragmentation.
Geographical Barriers and Corridors: Natural features like rivers,
mountains, and valleys serve as barriers or corridors that influence
animal movement and gene flow. Conservation planning uses this
knowledge to create wildlife corridors.
Human-Environment Interaction: Geography also considers
how local communities use land, water, and forests. Sustainable
practices vary with geography, such as terrace farming in the hills or
agroforestry in the plains.

sections.title: Challenges Faced by People Living in Forests
sections.content:
People living in forests often struggle to access essential facilities
such as healthcare, education, and clean water. Women are
exposed to fuelwood fumes and face, many health issues, making
their daily lives difficult. Forest dwellers depend heavily on forest
produce such as firewood, honey, bamboo, and medicinal plants
for their livelihood. Restrictions on forest use, deforestation, and
the commercial exploitation of resources often limit their access to
these resources. This creates a conflict between conservation laws
and their survival needs, leading to economic insecurity.
Forested hilly regions are prone to natural disasters such as floods
and landslides. Floods can wash away homes, crops, and roads, while
landslides can bury villages and cut off access to essential services.
Forest fires can quickly spread through dense vegetation, destroying
homes and resources. Human care and preventive measures can
help prevent many forest fires.
Crops are often damaged by elephants, monkeys, or wild boars, and
sometimes people face direct attacks. Such conflicts not only cause
economic losses but also create fear and insecurity among forest
communities.
Many forest dwellers also face discrimination and neglect from
mainstream society. They are often engaged in selling forest
products at relatively low prices. Therefore, creating opportunities
for processing and marketing these products is essential to
enhance their income. Forest communities also require assistance
in accessing government schemes and programmes, as well as
greater awareness of their legal rights.

sections.title: Government Efforts to Support Forest Dwellers
sections.content:
To reduce the hardships of people living in forests, the Government
of India has taken several steps. One of the most important measures
is the Scheduled Tribes and Other Traditional Forest Dwellers
(Recognition of Forest Rights) Act, 2006, commonly called the Forest
Rights Act (FRA). The Act recognises the rights of eligible communities
over the forest land and forest resources that they have traditionally
depended upon. It allows them to collect minor forest produce such
as bamboo, honey, and medicinal plants, and grants ownership of
small patches of land cultivated by them.

 Along with the FRA, the Government runs schemes for tribal
welfare, including education scholarships, healthcare programmes,
and skill development initiatives. The Joint Forest Management
(JFM) programme encourages local communities to participate
in protecting forests while benefiting from forest produce. Other
initiatives, such as the Panchayats (Extension to Scheduled Areas) Act
(PESA), the Dharti Aaba Janjatiya Gram Utkarsh Abhiyan (DAJGUA),
and the Pradhan Mantri Janjati Adivasi Nyaya Maha Abhiyan (PM
JANMAN), aim to promote the welfare of such communities.

Mendha Lekha: A Case Study in Community Forest
Management
Mendha Lekha is a small tribal village located in the Gadchiroli
district of Maharashtra, known for its effective communitybased forest management and self-governance. The village,
inhabited mainly by the Gond tribe, became the first in India
to gain rights over its forest resources under the Forest Rights
Act (2006). The people of Mendha Lekha follow the principle of
Mawa Nate Mawa Raj (our village, our rule), ensuring that all
decisions are made collectively through the Gram Sabha. They
protect and sustainably utilise their 1,800 hectares of forest by
regulating tree cutting, preventing forest fires, and promoting bamboo
harvesting as a renewable resource. The revenue from the forest
produce is used for community welfare activities such as education
and infrastructure. This also upholds the fundamental rights of
the people to participate in governance and control resources that
sustain their livelihoods. Simultaneously, the villagers fulfil their
fundamental duties by protecting biodiversity and preventing illegal
exploitation. This model has not only strengthened local livelihoods
but also demonstrates how traditional knowledge, rights, and duties,
as well as democratic participation, can coexist to achieve sustainable
forest conservation ().

The period between 1000 CE and 1700 CE witnessed profound
political, social, and cultural changes. The Indian subcontinent
experienced repeated invasions and wars accompanied by religious
discrimination and social distress. Regional powers frequently
resisted invaders who were making inroads into their territories.
This resistance took both military and cultural forms. Nonetheless,
this period manifested the resilience of the Indian civilisation,
which safeguarded its core ideas and values. Indian society not
only defended itself from external threats but also preserved its
traditions. In this chapter, we will see how resistance and resilience
shaped this period of Indian history.
Let us begin by understanding the meaning of resistance and
resilience in the context of the period under study and how they are
interconnected.
Resilience refers to the capacity to, survive and adapt in challenging
situations, including times of political unrest and instability. It is also
about how communities and groups across diverse regions respond
to challenges and opportunities. This capacity to absorb and adapt
to hardship while preserving inherited socio-cultural and spiritual
traditions can also be understood as resilience. The idea of India's
resilient spirit extends beyond political and military spheres.

Vijayanagara Empire: Resilience
against Expansion
Resistance to foreign invasions was not confined to northern India.
In the Deccan and beyond, the expanding campaigns of the Delhi
Sultanate steadily weakened the older kingdoms of the south. Malik
Kafur, Alauddin Khilji's general, attacked major cities and temples,
including those at Warangal, Belur, and Madurai. Later, Muhammad
bin Tughlaq's rise to power extended the Sultanate's influence even
farther south, ultimately contributing to the decline of the Pandya
Kingdom and the eventual emergence of a new sultanate territory
known as the Madurai Sultanate.
It was against this backdrop that the Vijayanagara Empire rose
in 1336 to check the expansion of the Sultanate into peninsular
India. Harihara and Bukka established the independent kingdom of
Vijayanagara-meaning 'City of Victory'-located near present-day
Hampi, Karnataka. The region's geography, including a formidable
river and rugged, rocky terrain, provided Vijayanagara with a strong
natural defence and a secure base for military operations. They
made determined efforts to defend and expand their state's frontiers.
The empire gradually expanded by annexing territory south of the
Krishna and Tungabhadra rivers and became one of the richest and
most influential states, encouraging the flourishing of literature in
Kannada, Telugu, Tamil, and Sanskrit. Vijayanagara's capital city
became a centre of trade, culture, and political power in southern
India.

Political Resilience
A major spiritual movement was founded by Guru Nanak in the late
15th century which later came to be known as Sikhism. It emphasised
devotion to one God, social equality, and the rejection of rituals.
Under Guru Nanak and his successors, the Sikh community expanded
and flourished across the subcontinent, particularly in the Punjab,
Sindh, and Gangetic plains. During this period, Punjab was largely
under the Lodi Sultans and later under the Mughals. It was a fertile,
densely populated region, with a large peasant population.

sections.title: Jat Resistance
sections.content:
During the 17th century, the Jats, a farming community from Ganga-
Yamuna Doab were burdened with heavy taxes and exploitation by
Mughals. These economic hardships combined with Aurangzeb's
religious policies led to growing resentment amongst the Jats. In
1669, under the leadership of Gokul Jat, they rebelled against the
Mughal Empire. Mughal forces struggled for many months to suppress
the uprising.
However, the Jats continued their resistance. In 1686, they took
advantage of Aurangzeb's prolonged military campaigns in the Deccan
and rebelled once again under the leadership of the zamindars of
Sinsani and Sogar. The Mughals sent several armies to suppress the
rebellion, leading to a long and fierce struggle in which both sides
suffered heavy losses. By 1691, the Mughals had gained the upper hand.
Yet, the Jat resistance continued.

sections.title: Temples
sections.content:
Temples functioned as central pillars of the region's socio-economic
and political life. These religious institutions evolved into major
economic hubs that managed extensive land grants, provided
employment to hundreds of specialised workers, and served as
financial institutions for local traders. Rulers used temple patronage
to strengthen their political legitimacy. Beyond their spiritual and
religious functions, temples facilitated social integration and served
as centres of education and culture, where artistic traditions such
as Bharatanatyam and many other art forms were preserved. They
also exercised quasi-judicial authority, collecting local taxes and
administering legal penalties.
Temples also served as sources of legitimacy for political authority.
The deities of these temples were regarded as protectors of the state
and its people. In some cases, the deity was regarded as the ruler,
while the actual ruler governed as the deity's deputy. For example,
the Gajapati rulers of Odisha called themselves the Rauta (deputy)
of Jagannath. Similarly, the Kachhwaha rulers of Jaipur governed on
behalf of Govindadevaji, while the Rajput rulers of Kota regarded
themselves as representatives of Rama.
Temples in India also functioned as significant economic
institutions. They provided employment to a wide range of groups,
including architects, artisans, sculptors, priests, musicians, and
administrative staff. As substantial landholders, temples received
donations, endowments, and land grants, often given as acts of

The terms 'government' and 'governance' are closely related.
However, they are not synonymous. Government refers to the
institutions and authorities that exercise political power, while
governance refers to the process by which decisions are made,
implemented, and monitored in the public interest. The government
formulates and implements people-centric policies, and good
governance ensures that these policies are transparent, accountable,
effective, and responsive to people's needs. Governance is the system
through which decisions are made, implemented, and monitored for
the welfare of the people. It refers to the way a country, state, city,
village, school, or organisation is managed. Therefore, understanding
governance is essential to know how government impacts our lives.

sections.title: Evolution of Governance in India
sections.content:
In the previous section, we studied that while the government is
the institutional aspect, governance refers to its functional aspect.
The government's institutional setup influences the nature of
governance, and governance initiatives, in turn, require institutional
adaptations to implement policies and schemes.
We are familiar with the structure of government at different levels
in India. But the same structure has not always existed as it does
now; it has evolved from certain historical experiences. Let us
understand this historical context by looking at the 'big picture' of
the world history.
Do you remember the phenomenon of colonialism that you learnt
about in Grade 8? We know that European powers colonised many
societies, particularly those in Asia, Africa, and the Americas.
Before colonial rulers forced their own models of governance
and policy-making on colonised people, these societies governed
themselves in accordance with local and organic systems. Although
most colonies had become independent by the end of the 20th
century, colonial institutions largely persisted, and their structures
continued to dominate even in contemporary times. India is not
an exception to the historical legacy of colonialism. However, India
stands out in two important ways. Firstly, unlike many societies that
experienced colonial rule, India has preserved most of its knowledge
of its pre-colonial institutions and traditions of governance through
texts and practices. Secondly, after Independence in 1947, it was not
possible to replace all colonial institutions at once. The leaders of
independent India therefore framed the Constitution in the spirit of
India's own values and ideals.

The task of governance is always ongoing. With time, the needs,
desires, and aspirations of people also evolve, creating new challenges
to which the government and the institutions have to respond.
For example, weak coordination between different institutions
and departments can affect the implementation of government
programmes. At the same time, unequal access to public services

sections.title: The Making of a Public Policy
sections.content:
A public policy is developed through a systematic process rather
than a single decision. It usually begins when citizens, government
officials, researchers, or civil society organisations realise that a
new need has to be met, an existing problem has to be resolved, or
a facility has to be made better in the interest of the people. Then
the government studies the issue, collects information, and consults
experts, stakeholders, and the public to understand different
viewpoints and possible solutions. Based on these discussions,
the government authorities prepare, review, and approve a draft
policy. Once the policy is approved by the concerned authorities,
it is translated into programmes and schemes, which provide a
clear framework for different ministries, departments, and local
governments to take specific action. The implementation of any
policy is continuously monitored and evaluated to assess whether
it is achieving its objectives. Feedback from citizens and other
stakeholders is used to improve the policy over time. Thus, public
policy is a continuous cycle of problem identification, consultation,
policy formulation, implementation, monitoring, evaluation, and
improvement. This process helps the government respond effectively
to the changing needs of society.

. Common investment options

a) Fixed Deposits (FDs)
Fixed deposits are among the most common and safest investment
options offered by banks and post offices. In a fixed deposit, a
person deposits a lump sum amount for a fixed period, such as one,
three, or five years. During this period, the bank or post office pays
a fixed rate of interest on this amount, which remains unchanged
throughout the investment period. Fixed deposits offer assured
returns and are suitable for people who prefer safety over high
returns.
Other government-backed investment options include the Public
Provident Fund (PPF) and small savings schemes, such as the National
Savings Certificate (NSC) and the Sukanya Samriddhi Yojana. These
schemes encourage long-term savings while providing safe and
reasonable returns.

b) Bonds
Bonds are investments through which people lend money to the
government or companies (issuers of bonds) for a fixed period.
Bondholders earn regular interest. For example, if you buy a bond
worth ₹10,000 that pays 5% interest per year, you will receive ₹500
as interest after one year. If the bond matures after one year, you
will receive ₹10,500 in total. In reality, the maturity period ranges
from 1 day to 30 years or more. You may also be able to sell the
bond before maturity if you need the money earlier, making them
more liquid. Government bonds are generally considered safer
than corporate bonds and are suitable for those seeking a stable,
predictable income.

of its savings for the expenses incurred towards the treatment.

Types of Insurance

Health Insurance

Health insurance helps cover medical expenses, such as hospitalisation,

b)

Life Insurance

Life insurance provides financial support to a family if the policyholder,
who may be the breadwinner of the family, passes away. It helps dependents

insurance is an important tool for ensuring long-term financial security.

General Insurance

 India's Traditional Entrepreneurial Community
Entrepreneurship in India has deep roots among traditional communities,
where skills, occupations, and occupational knowledge have been
passed down through generations. Long before modern startups, these
communities practised self-employment, innovation, and trade, forming
the backbone of India's local economy.
The Chettiar (Nattukottai Chettiar) community from Tamil Nadu
is a well-known traditional entrepreneurial community. Historically,
Chettiars were traders, bankers, and moneylenders, operating not only
across India but also in Sri Lanka, Burma (now Myanmar), Malaysia, and
other parts of Southeast Asia. They were known for:



Strong business ethics and trust-based lending



Excellent accounting and record-keeping skills



Reinvesting profits into trade, temples, education, and community
welfare

The Chettiar community built wealth through trade in salt, rice,
textiles, and finance, often without formal banks. Even today, Chettiar
entrepreneurship inspires modern India by showing how risk-taking,
discipline, and long-term vision can build sustainable businesses rooted

sections.content:
India's vibrant startup ecosystem is built not only on innovation but
also on perseverance. All entrepreneurs should be aware that there
is a chance of their business ending in failure. So while some startups
grow rapidly, others struggle or even close down. As with other things
in life, there is nothing wrong with failure if an honest effort has
been made. Hence, these experiences contribute to entrepreneurial
learning, and every unsuccessful attempt offers lessons that help
entrepreneurs develop stronger ideas and build
better businesses in the future.

agri-tech (farming technology). Cities like Bengaluru, Hyderabad,
Mumbai, and Delhi NCR have become major startup hubs. These

economic growth.
In recognition of the importance of promoting entrepreneurship, the
government has introduced many schemes, such as Startup India,
which supports the vision of Atmanirbhar Bharat, focusing on
making India self-reliant through innovation and local solutions.
As India moves towards the vision of Viksit Bharat 2047,

employment, driving innovation, empowering communities, and

meaningful difference to society.
